title: Public and Global Health
tagline: Determinants of health, prevention, screening, vaccination programmes, global health and health systems
summary: The health of populations depends as much on living conditions and policy as on medical care. This course covers the determinants of health and health inequalities, prevention and health promotion, screening and vaccination programmes, the control of communicable and non-communicable disease, environmental and occupational health, global health, and health systems and economics, with UK arrangements as the main example.
overview: Public health is the work of protecting and improving the health of whole populations. Most of the gains in life expectancy over the past two centuries came from clean water and sanitation, better housing and nutrition, vaccination, safer roads and workplaces, and tobacco control, rather than from treating individual patients. Public health uses epidemiology and statistics as its methods, and programmes, policies and services as its tools.

The course begins with how health is distributed: the social determinants of health, how inequalities are measured, and why the social gradient matters. It then covers prevention and health promotion, including Rose's population strategy and behaviour change; screening, with its criteria, test performance, biases and overdiagnosis, and the UK national programmes; vaccination programmes, herd immunity and vaccine confidence; and the control of communicable disease, from surveillance and outbreak investigation to the International Health Regulations.

Later chapters deal with non-communicable disease and its main risk factors (tobacco, alcohol, diet, obesity and physical inactivity); environmental and occupational health, including air pollution, heat, lead, radon and occupational disease; global health, including the burden of disease, maternal and child health, antimicrobial resistance and universal health coverage; and health systems and economics, including QALYs, cost-effectiveness, NICE and how the NHS is financed and organised. Each chapter has worked examples and calculations. Figures and policies are dated, because they change.
outcomes: Describe the social determinants of health, measure health inequalities with absolute and relative measures and the slope index of inequality, and explain why structural interventions tend to reduce inequalities more than individual ones.

Distinguish the levels of prevention and the population and high-risk strategies, calculate numbers needed to treat and attributable fractions, and describe the evidence for major health promotion interventions.
Apply the criteria for screening, calculate predictive values, explain lead-time bias, length bias and overdiagnosis, and describe the UK national screening programmes and their eligibility.
Explain herd immunity and the herd immunity threshold, describe how vaccination programmes are designed, monitored and evaluated, and discuss vaccine hesitancy and how to respond to it.
Describe surveillance and notification, the steps of an outbreak investigation, contact tracing, isolation and quarantine, and the International Health Regulations.
Summarise the burden and main risk factors of non-communicable disease and the evidence for policies on tobacco, alcohol, diet and physical activity, including taxation and regulation.

Describe the health effects of air pollution, climate change, lead, radon and carbon monoxide, apply the hierarchy of control and UK occupational health law, calculate noise exposure, and take an occupational history.

Use DALYs and the main measures of maternal and child mortality, explain the epidemiological transition, antimicrobial resistance and One Health, and describe the global health institutions and universal health coverage.
Calculate QALYs, ICERs and net monetary benefit, explain opportunity cost and NICE's use of thresholds, and compare the ways health systems are financed and providers are paid.

history.title: An occupational cancer described
history.detail: Percivall Pott describes scrotal cancer in London chimney sweeps who had worked in chimneys as children, and attributes it to soot. It was the first cancer linked to an occupational exposure.

history.title: Vaccination begins
history.detail: Edward Jenner inoculates James Phipps with material from a cowpox lesion and later shows that he is protected against smallpox. His work, published in 1798, led to vaccination programmes and, nearly two centuries later, to the eradication of smallpox.

history.title: The sanitary report
history.detail: Edwin Chadwick's Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population of Great Britain links disease and early death to poor drainage, water supply and housing. It led to the Public Health Act 1848 and the building of sewers and clean water supplies.

history.title: Cholera and the Broad Street pump
history.detail: John Snow maps cases of cholera in Soho around a water pump in Broad Street and compares death rates between customers of two water companies, showing that cholera is spread by contaminated water decades before its cause was identified.

history.title: The WHO and the NHS
history.detail: The World Health Organization is founded on 7 April 1948, and the National Health Service begins on 5 July 1948, providing care to everyone in the UK free at the point of use.

history.title: The Black Report
history.detail: The Working Group on Inequalities in Health, chaired by Sir Douglas Black and set up in 1977, reports that the gap in health between social classes is large and mainly explained by material conditions. Its findings shaped later research and policy on health inequalities.

history.title: Smallpox eradicated
history.detail: The World Health Assembly declares smallpox eradicated, after a WHO programme that combined vaccination with surveillance and containment around cases. It remains the only human disease to have been eradicated.

history.title: The Ottawa Charter
history.detail: The first International Conference on Health Promotion adopts the Ottawa Charter, with five areas for action: build healthy public policy, create supportive environments, strengthen community action, develop personal skills and reorient health services.

history.title: The Sustainable Development Goals
history.detail: UN member states adopt the 2030 Agenda. Goal 3 includes targets to reduce maternal and child deaths, end epidemics of AIDS, tuberculosis and malaria, reduce premature mortality from non-communicable diseases by one-third, and achieve universal health coverage.

references.title: Oxford Textbook of Global Public Health
references.authors: Roger Detels, Quarraisha Abdool Karim, Fran Baum, Liming Li and Alastair H. Leyland (eds)
references.note: Seventh edition. A comprehensive reference on the scope, methods and practice of public health worldwide.

references.title: Donaldsons' Essential Public Health
references.authors: Liam J. Donaldson and Paul D. Rutter
references.note: Fourth edition. A concise introduction to public health with a UK focus, covering epidemiology, health protection, health improvement and health services.

references.title: Rose's Strategy of Preventive Medicine
references.authors: Geoffrey Rose, with commentary by Kay-Tee Khaw and Michael Marmot
references.note: Rose's 1992 classic on the population and high-risk strategies of prevention and the prevention paradox.

references.title: Principles and Practice of Screening for Disease
references.authors: J. M. G. Wilson and G. Jungner
references.note: WHO Public Health Papers No. 34. The source of the classic criteria for screening programmes.

references.title: Immunisation against Infectious Disease (the Green Book)
references.note: The UK reference on vaccines and vaccination procedures; individual chapters are updated online as schedules change.

references.title: Fair Society, Healthy Lives: The Marmot Review
references.note: The strategic review of health inequalities in England, which introduced proportionate universalism and six policy objectives.

references.title: Hunter's Diseases of Occupations
references.authors: Peter J. Baxter, Tar-Ching Aw, Anne Cockcroft, Paul Durrington and J. Malcolm Harrington (eds)
references.note: Tenth edition. The standard reference on occupational disease, exposures and their prevention.

references.title: Methods for the Economic Evaluation of Health Care Programmes
references.authors: Michael F. Drummond, Mark J. Sculpher, Karl Claxton, Greg L. Stoddart and George W. Torrance
references.note: Fourth edition. The standard text on cost-effectiveness and cost-utility analysis, QALYs and decision modelling.
